nodes.label: Mountain food
nodes.answer: Eat small amounts frequently, prioritize carbohydrates during sustained effort, use calorie-dense foods for multi-day trips, and maintain hydration and electrolyte balance.

nodes.label: Hiking nutrition
nodes.answer: Fuel hiking with a mix of carbohydrates for immediate energy, protein for recovery, and fats for sustained calorie density. Eat small portions regularly and match food and fluid intake to the duration, intensity, and weather.

nodes.label: Calories
nodes.answer: Calorie needs rise with distance, elevation gain, pack weight, cold weather, and exertion. For demanding mountain days, plan generous high-calorie food and always carry a reserve in case of delays or an emergency.

nodes.label: Carbohydrates
nodes.answer: Carbohydrates are the main fast fuel for sustained hiking. Eat roughly 30-60 grams of carbohydrates per hour on longer or harder efforts, using foods such as dried fruit, bread, wraps, oats, rice, or energy bars.

nodes.label: Protein
nodes.answer: Include protein in meals and snacks to support satiety and muscle repair. Good trail options include nuts, seeds, cheese, jerky, nut butter, eggs, and beans, though fresh foods need careful packing and temperature management.

nodes.label: Fats
nodes.answer: Fats provide more than twice the energy per gram of carbohydrate or protein, making them useful for lightweight, calorie-dense mountain food. Combine nuts, seeds, nut butter, cheese, or oil with carbohydrate sources for balanced energy.

nodes.label: Hydration
nodes.answer: Drink regularly throughout the day rather than waiting until you are very thirsty. Sip small amounts every 15-30 minutes, increase intake in heat or at altitude, and check that your urine remains pale rather than dark.

nodes.label: Electrolytes
nodes.answer: On long, hot, or high-sweat outings, replace sodium and other electrolytes as well as water. Use electrolyte tablets, powder, or a sports drink, especially if you are drinking large volumes of plain water.

nodes.label: Trail snacks
nodes.answer: Pack a variety of snacks you enjoy and can eat while moving: nuts, dried fruit, trail mix, energy bars, chocolate, crackers, cheese, or jerky. Aim for small, frequent snacks rather than one heavy lunch.

nodes.label: Energy bars
nodes.answer: Energy bars are convenient, but choose ones you can digest comfortably and that provide useful carbohydrates, some protein, and enough calories. Carry at least one spare bar for delays, cold weather, or an unplanned bivouac.

nodes.label: Trail breakfast
phrases: what to eat before a hike
nodes.answer: Eat a familiar, balanced breakfast with carbohydrates, some protein, and a little fat, and start hydrating early. Oats, bread, eggs, fruit, yogurt, or nut butter are practical options depending on trip length and facilities.

nodes.label: Trail lunch
nodes.answer: Choose a lunch that is easy to eat in wind, cold, or rain, such as wraps, bread with cheese or nut butter, dried fruit, and nuts. On hot days, avoid foods that spoil quickly and keep perishables shaded and cool.

nodes.label: Trail dinner
nodes.answer: For overnight trips, plan a hot, calorie-rich dinner with a carbohydrate base plus protein and fat, such as pasta, rice, or couscous with cheese, sausage, beans, or dehydrated meal ingredients. A warm meal and drink also help with morale and thermoregulation.

nodes.label: Calorie density
nodes.answer: For long trips, favor calorie-dense foods such as nuts, oil, cheese, chocolate, nut butter, and dehydrated meals to reduce weight and bulk. Balance them with enough carbohydrate and fiber for comfortable digestion and steady energy.

nodes.label: Food packing
nodes.answer: Pack food in durable, resealable bags or containers, keep it accessible during the day, and protect it from rain and crushing. In wildlife areas, follow local rules for bear canisters, hangs, or other approved storage, and pack out all waste.

nodes.label: Food safety
nodes.answer: Keep perishable food cool, discard anything that has spoiled, and wash or sanitize hands before eating. Treat or filter water from natural sources unless you are certain it is safe, and avoid cross-contamination between raw and ready-to-eat food.

nodes.label: Water treatment
nodes.answer: Treat water from streams, lakes, or unreliable taps with a filter, chemical treatment, boiling, or UV purification. Carry a backup method, because filters can freeze, clog, break, or fail when you need them most.

nodes.label: Altitude and appetite
nodes.answer: At altitude, appetite and digestion can decrease even as energy needs remain high. Eat familiar, easy-to-digest foods in small frequent portions, prioritize fluids and carbohydrates, and do not skip meals because you feel less hungry.

nodes.label: Cold weather food
nodes.answer: In cold weather, plan extra calories, warm meals, and hot drinks, and keep food close to your body so it does not freeze. Choose foods that remain edible when cold and carry sufficient stove fuel for melting snow if needed.

nodes.label: Hot weather food
nodes.answer: In hot weather, drink consistently, replace electrolytes, and choose foods that will not spoil quickly. Salty snacks can help maintain sodium balance, while fruit and moist foods can contribute useful fluids.

nodes.label: Eating schedule
nodes.answer: Eat a small snack every 30-60 minutes during sustained hiking instead of waiting until you feel exhausted. Regular fueling helps prevent energy crashes, poor decision-making, and the heavy fatigue often called bonking.

nodes.label: Emergency food
nodes.answer: Always carry extra high-calorie, shelf-stable food beyond your planned meals. Energy bars, nuts, dried fruit, and chocolate are compact reserves for delays, route changes, cold weather, or an unexpected night outdoors.

nodes.label: Food allergies and diets
nodes.answer: Plan around allergies and dietary needs before leaving, read labels carefully, and carry safe alternatives for every meal and snack. If hiking in a group, agree on shared-food rules to prevent accidental exposure.

nodes.label: Food planning
nodes.answer: Plan food by trip length, expected exertion, weather, water availability, and cooking facilities. Make a simple menu of breakfast, lunch, dinner, snacks, drinks, and emergency reserves, then check that the total calories and weight are realistic.

nodes.label: Leave No Trace food
nodes.answer: Pack out all food wrappers, scraps, and waste, and never feed wildlife. Store food securely, minimize odors, and leave campsites and rest stops cleaner than you found them.

nodes.label: Cooking equipment
nodes.answer: Choose a cooking system appropriate for the trip: no-cook food for short outings, a compact stove for hot meals, and a reliable stove plus windscreen for winter or exposed camps. Always carry an independent ignition backup and enough fuel.

nodes.label: Caffeine
nodes.answer: Caffeine can improve alertness, but use it in moderation and do not let it replace water, food, or sleep. Avoid excessive caffeine late in the day if it may interfere with recovery or overnight sleep.

nodes.label: Recovery nutrition
nodes.answer: After a long hike, rehydrate, replace electrolytes, and eat a meal containing carbohydrates and protein. This supports fluid balance, glycogen replenishment, and muscle recovery before the next day’s activity.
